n: Job compares human life to hard military service or the life of a hired laborer — long, tiring, and under someone else’s control.

f.g: Literally “hard service,” like a soldier’s term of duty.
A hired day laborer.

n: Like a slave longing for evening shade or a worker waiting for his wages, Job longs for relief.

f.g: The shade of evening, when work ends.

n: Instead, he has been given months of emptiness and nights of misery.

f.g: Emptiness, futility.

n: At night he can’t sleep, tossing and turning until dawn, wishing the night would end. Anyone who has suffered sleepless nights will recognize this.

f.g: Restless turning in bed.

n: His body is covered with worms and scabs; his skin cracks and oozes. Job describes his disease in painful detail.

f.g: Crusty scabs.
Running with pus; disgusting.

n: His days fly by faster than a weaver’s shuttle, and they run out without hope. In Hebrew, “hope” can also mean “thread” — his life is ending like a thread run out.

f.g: The tool that carries thread quickly back and forth on a loom.
A wordplay: Hebrew tiqvah means both “hope” and “thread.”

n: Job now speaks directly to God: remember that my life is just a breath; I’ll never see good again.
Soon no one will see him again. “You will look for me, but I will be gone.”

f.w: thine eyes are upon me, and I am not
f.g: You will look for me, but I will no longer exist.

n: Like a cloud that disappears, someone who goes down to the grave does not come back up. At this low point Job sees no hope beyond death; later he will reach toward a hope of resurrection (Job 14:14; 19:25-26).

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

n: He will never return home, and his own house will forget him.

f.w: neither shall his place know him any more

n: So Job won’t hold back. He will speak out of the anguish and bitterness of his soul. His honest complaint is itself a kind of prayer.

f.w: I will not refrain my mouth

n: Am I the raging sea or a sea monster that you must keep me under guard? In ancient imagery, the sea and its monsters were forces of chaos that God restrained.

f.g: Hebrew tannin — a sea monster or dragon, symbol of chaos.

n: When he hopes his bed will give him some comfort...
...God terrifies him with nightmares and visions. Even sleep offers no escape.

f.g: Frightens me with nightmares.

n: He would rather be strangled than continue living like this.

f.g: Suffocation, death.

n: I hate my life; I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone — my days are only a breath.

f.g: I don’t want to live forever.
A breath, vapor — fleeting.

n: Job twists the words of Psalm 8. The psalmist marveled that God cares for mankind; Job asks why God pays so much attention to him — it feels like scrutiny, not love.

f.w: What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?

n: Why inspect him every morning and test him every moment? Job feels constantly examined.

f.g: Inspect, examine.
Test.

n: How long until you look away and let me alone even long enough to swallow? A vivid Hebrew idiom for “just a moment’s break.”

f.w: till I swallow down my spittle
f.g: An idiom: not even a moment’s rest.

n: Even if I have sinned, what have I done to you, you watcher of humankind? Why make me your target? Job does not admit guilt, but asks why any sin of his would matter so much.

f.g: Literally “watcher of men” — here with a bitter edge.
A target.

n: Why not just forgive me? Soon I will lie in the dust; you will look for me and I’ll be gone. Even in his complaint, Job assumes God would miss him — a glimmer of the relationship he still believes in.

f.w: why dost thou not pardon my transgression
thou shalt seek me in the morning
f.g: Job imagines God searching for him after he dies.
